results.title: Global Assessment of the Relationship Between Breast Cancer Risk and Dietary Intake: An Ecological Study.
results.journal: American journal of health promotion : AJHP
results.first_screen_reason: The ecological study directly assesses alcohol consumption in relation to breast cancer incidence and reports a positive association.
results.reason: The study remains relevant, but no complete Good-quality quantitative extraction could be verified from the available abstract and accessible full text.

extraction.comparison_type: Continuous country-level alcohol intake associated with age-standardized breast cancer incidence
extraction.timing: Country-level dietary intake and incidence data from global databases; temporal relationship unclear
extraction.supporting_text: The study included data from 175 countries and reported that alcohol consumption remained positively associated with breast cancer incidence after adjustment and Bonferroni correction (β=0.209, P=0.048).

results.title: Global Burden, Quality of Care, and Attributable Risk Factors of Young-Onset Breast Cancer (YOBC) by WHO Regions: A Systematic Analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019.
results.first_screen_reason: The study evaluates young-onset breast cancer incidence and the burden attributable to alcohol consumption.
results.reason: The study remains relevant, but no complete Good-quality quantitative extraction could be verified from the available abstract and accessible full text.

extraction.design: Ecological time-trend analysis of Global Burden of Disease data
extraction.supporting_text: The authors retrieved Global Burden of Disease 1990-2019 data and evaluated young-onset breast cancer incidence and attribution to each risk factor; they report 168,775 new cases in 2019 and describe a shift in burden attributable to alcohol consumption.

results.title: Association of Smoking and Alcohol Consumption with Female Reproductive Diseases: A Mendelian Randomization Study on the Mediating Role of Circulating Metabolites.
results.first_screen_reason: The Mendelian randomization study explicitly evaluates alcohol consumption in relation to female reproductive disorders including endometrioid ovarian cancer risk.
results.reason: This two-sample Mendelian-randomization study reported a quantitative association between genetically predicted weekly alcohol consumption and endometrioid ovarian cancer risk and should be recorded separately from conventional studies.

extraction.comparison_type: Higher genetically predicted drinks per week versus lower genetically predicted drinks per week
extraction.design: Two-sample Mendelian randomization using GSCAN exposure GWAS and outcome GWAS summary data
extraction.timing: Genetic predisposition representing lifelong alcohol consumption
extraction.exposure_measurement_type: Genetic instrumental variables for drinks per week
extraction.supporting_text: Weekly alcohol consumption exhibited a negative association with endometrioid ovarian cancer (OR = 0.48, 95% CI [0.31–0.74], P = 0.001).

results.title: Comparative analysis of breast cancer burden in China, India, and the United States.
results.first_screen_reason: The study analyzes female breast cancer incidence and explicitly identifies high red meat intake as a leading breast cancer risk factor in China.
results.reason: The GBD ecological risk-attribution analysis identifies high red-meat intake as a breast-cancer risk in China but reports no context-specific RR, OR, or HR with uncertainty and does not achieve a Good JBI grade.

extraction.design: Ecological GBD modeling and risk-attribution analysis
extraction.exposure_measurement_type: Modeled dietary exposure from the GBD comparative risk assessment framework
extraction.supporting_text: Attribution analysis identified a diet high in red meat as a representative risk factor in China, but no exposure-category contrast or red-meat-specific effect estimate with uncertainty was reported.

results.title: Temporal trends in behavioural risk factors for cancers with rising incidence in younger adults: an analysis of population-based data in England.
results.first_screen_reason: The study plausibly evaluates alcohol and other behavioral factors in relation to ovarian cancer incidence trends and attributable risk.
results.reason: Full text states that the alcohol-linked cancers were liver, colorectal, oral, and breast cancer, so it provides no alcohol–ovarian cancer incidence analysis.

extraction.design: Ecological population-based repeated cross-sectional time-trend study using national cancer registry and health survey data
extraction.timing: Cancer incidence 2001–2019; alcohol trends assessed through 2019, with moderate and heavy drinking trends reported from 2011–2019
extraction.exposure_measurement_type: Self-reported alcohol consumption from population-based national health surveys
extraction.supporting_text: The article states that only four selected cancers were linked with alcohol—“liver, colorectal, oral, breast”—excluding ovarian cancer; relative risks used for PAF calculations were obtained from prior literature rather than estimated from study participants.

results.title: The Mediating Role of Serum Phosphate in the BMI-Breast Cancer Association: A Prospective Study from the UK Biobank.
results.first_screen_reason: This prospective cohort directly evaluates baseline serum phosphate, a biomarker of phosphorus status, in relation to breast cancer risk.
results.reason: The study remains relevant, but no complete Good-quality quantitative extraction could be verified from the available abstract and accessible full text.

extraction.timing: Serum phosphate was measured at baseline before incident breast cancer assessment; prior or early tumor diagnoses were excluded.
extraction.supporting_text: A total of 198,280 women from the UK Biobank were enrolled in this prospective cohort analysis; serum phosphate levels were measured at baseline, and phosphate levels appeared to have a protective effect on breast cancer risk.

results.title: Breast Cancer Burden in BRICS Countries Attributable to Smoking, High Alcohol Use, High Body Mass Index, and Low Physical Activity, 1990-2021: Findings from the Global Burden of Disease 2021 and Mendelian Randomization.
results.first_screen_reason: The study explicitly assesses high alcohol use as a potentially causal risk factor for female breast cancer burden.
results.reason: This two-sample Mendelian-randomization analysis reports a quantitative association between genetically proxied high alcohol use and breast cancer incidence and must be recorded separately from conventional studies.

extraction.comparison_type: higher versus lower genetic liability to alcohol use disorder/high alcohol use
extraction.timing: genetically proxied exposure; no conventional follow-up period
extraction.supporting_text: The primary IVW analysis using 94 SNPs reported OR=1.03 (95% CI 1.03–1.03); Figure 5 reports P<0.001. Cochran's Q, MR-Egger intercept, MR-PRESSO, and leave-one-out analyses found no evidence of heterogeneity, directional pleiotropy, or influential outliers.

results.title: Global burden of breast cancer and its association with red meat consumption: spatiotemporal trends, projections, and triangulation of evidence.
results.first_screen_reason: The article directly examines red meat consumption in relation to breast cancer risk and incidence.
results.reason: This two-sample Mendelian-randomization analysis reported a quantitative association between genetically predicted higher beef intake and breast cancer incidence and must be recorded separately from conventional studies.

extraction.comparison_type: Genetically predicted higher versus lower beef intake, mutually adjusted for beef, pork, and lamb consumption
extraction.timing: Exposure GWAS conducted in 2018; breast cancer outcome GWAS timing not reported
extraction.exposure_measurement_type: Genetic instruments for self-reported beef intake
extraction.supporting_text: In the multivariable MR analysis simultaneously adjusting for beef, pork, and lamb consumption, beef intake remained associated with breast cancer risk using IVW (OR = 3.39, 95% CI: 1.47–7.86, P = 0.004); BCAC included 122,977 cases and 105,974 controls.

results.title: Association between lifestyle and risk of early-onset cancer: Evidence from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition and the UK Biobank.
results.first_screen_reason: This prospective analysis directly evaluates alcohol consumption in relation to early-onset breast cancer risk, including a null association.
results.reason: The study remains relevant, but no complete Good-quality quantitative extraction could be verified from the available abstract and accessible full text.

extraction.comparison_type: One-point increase in alcohol score from 0 (most unfavourable) to 4 (most favourable)
extraction.design: Prospective cohort study combining EPIC and UK Biobank estimates
extraction.timing: Alcohol exposure assessed at cohort enrollment before incident cancer diagnosis
extraction.supporting_text: Participants enrolled before age 50 in EPIC and the UK Biobank were analysed; 1765 breast cancers occurred, and alcohol showed no association with breast cancer.

results.title: Changes in alcohol consumption and the risk of postmenopausal breast cancer in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition cohort.
results.first_screen_reason: The prospective cohort directly evaluates changes in alcohol consumption in relation to subsequent postmenopausal breast cancer risk.
results.reason: This Good-quality prospective cohort study reported a fully adjusted HR with 95% CI for incident postmenopausal breast cancer per 10 g/day increase in alcohol-consumption change.

extraction.comparison_type: Per 10 g/day increase in alcohol consumption change between baseline and follow-up assessments
extraction.timing: Alcohol intake was assessed at recruitment and a median 9.8 years later; incident breast cancer was then ascertained over a median 4.0 years
extraction.exposure_measurement_type: Repeated self-reported validated dietary or lifestyle questionnaires
extraction.supporting_text: Table 2 reported for overall breast cancer: 2,173 cases among 123,679 women; fully adjusted Model 2 HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.93–1.01) per 10 g/day change in alcohol consumption.

results.title: Association between risk-related lifestyle factors, screening adherence and breast cancer incidence: a decomposition analysis.

extraction.supporting_text: Among 10,579 women, 571 were diagnosed with breast cancer during follow-up; higher alcohol consumption had a total excess risk ratio of 1.55 (P<0.0001), but no confidence interval or exact contrast was reported.
